author: Cyprian of Carthage
occasion: Cyprian offers a sustained catechetical and pastoral explanation of the Lord's Prayer, teaching Christians how to pray and what the prayer's petitions mean for their life.
argument: Cyprian presents the Lord's Prayer as Christ's own gift and the perfect pattern of Christian prayer. He explains each petition in turn: calling God 'Father' marks our rebirth as God's children; praying 'our' Father binds the whole people in unity; the petitions for the hallowing of God's name, the coming of his kingdom, and the doing of his will teach us to seek holiness, heavenly glory, and obedience. The prayer for daily bread is understood both as the Eucharist and as contentment with daily provision. The prayer for forgiveness is tied to our own forgiveness of others, and the final petitions teach humility and reliance on God's protection against evil. Cyprian closes by urging constant, watchful, and fruitful prayer, joined with good works, at all hours.

outline.move: The gospel commands, especially the Lord's own teaching on prayer, are greater than the prophets; Christ gave the form of prayer so that we may be heard.
Prayer should be offered with quietness, modesty, and humility, as shown by Anna and the publican, not with noisy display.
The Lord's Prayer is given in full, and its first word 'our' teaches that prayer is public and communal, not private.
Calling God 'Father' confesses our rebirth as God's children, excludes the Jews who rejected Christ, and obliges us to live as God's children.
The petitions for the hallowing of God's name, the coming of his kingdom, and the doing of his will ask that these realities be accomplished in us.
God's will is humility, faith, justice, mercy, and love of Christ; it must be done in both body and spirit, and we pray it may be done even in unbelievers.
The prayer for daily bread is understood both as Christ the bread of life in the Eucharist and as contentment with daily provision, renouncing worldly wealth.
God provides for the righteous, as shown by Daniel and Elijah, so those who seek God's kingdom need not worry about daily food.
The prayer for forgiveness teaches us that we are daily sinners and binds our own forgiveness from God to our forgiveness of others; peace and concord are the true sacrifice.
The petition not to be led into temptation teaches humility and reliance on God, and the final petition for deliverance from evil sums up all our needs.
The prayer is a brief summary of all saving teaching; Christ himself prayed constantly and interceded for our unity.
Prayer requires a heart fixed on God, and prayer is made effective by good works, especially almsgiving.
The hours of prayer have expanded for Christians; since Christ is the true sun and day, we should pray without ceasing, night and day.

cast.name: Cyprian
cast.who: Bishop of Carthage and author of the treatise.

cast.name: Christ
cast.who: The Son of God, teacher of the Lord's Prayer, and the true bread of life.

cast.name: Anna
cast.who: The mother of Samuel, presented as a model of silent, heartfelt prayer.

cast.name: The publican
cast.who: The tax collector in Jesus' parable whose humble prayer was heard.

cast.name: The Pharisee
cast.who: The self-righteous man in the parable whose proud prayer was not justified.

cast.name: Abel
cast.who: The first martyr, whose peaceful and just sacrifice pleased God.

cast.name: Cain
cast.who: Abel's brother, whose discordant heart made his sacrifice unacceptable.

cast.name: Daniel
cast.who: The prophet fed by God in the lions' den.

cast.name: Elijah
cast.who: The prophet fed by ravens in the wilderness.

cast.name: Job
cast.who: The righteous man tested by Satan with God's permission.

cast.name: Cornelius
cast.who: The centurion whose prayers and almsgiving were heard by God.

cast.name: Raphael
cast.who: The angel who presented the prayers and good works of Tobit and Sarah before God.

cast.name: Tobit
cast.who: The righteous man whose prayers and burial of the dead were remembered by God.

cast.name: Sarah
cast.who: Tobit's daughter-in-law, whose prayer was heard.

cast.name: Peter
cast.who: The apostle for whom Christ prayed that his faith would not fail.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle whose writings Cyprian cites on the flesh, the spirit, and contentment.

cast.name: John
cast.who: The apostle and evangelist cited on sin and love of the world.

cast.name: Isaiah
cast.who: The prophet cited on Israel's rejection and on true fasting and almsgiving.

cast.name: Jeremiah
cast.who: The prophet cited on inward worship.

cast.name: Solomon
cast.who: The king whose sin gave Satan power against him.

cast.name: Nebuchadnezzar
cast.who: The king of Babylon to whom God gave Jerusalem.

cast.name: Judas
cast.who: The betrayer of Christ, whose example the discordant imitate.

cast.name: Epaphroditus
cast.who: The bearer of gifts from the Philippians to Paul.

Evil, especially the assaults of the devil and the world

scripture: Cyprian uses Old Latin biblical texts close to the Septuagint and early Latin gospel traditions. Psalm numbering follows the Septuagint/Vulgate. In modern form, cite Psalms according to the Hebrew numbering with a note where the Septuagint numbering differs. Old Testament books should be cited by their modern names: 'the first of Kingdoms' as 1 Samuel, 'Canticum canticorum' as Song of Songs. New Testament books are cited by their usual modern names.
uncertain: The exact date of composition; c. 252 is the common estimate but not certain from the text.
Whether Cyprian's biblical citations reflect a single Old Latin version or a mixture of versions.
The precise liturgical setting of the phrase 'sursum corda' in Cyprian's Carthage.
